title: Colour and rainbows: how sunlight splits into colours

summary.text: Sunlight looks white, but it is really many colours mixed together. A glass of water or a prism spreads them into red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, because each colour bends by a different amount. Raindrops do the same, and that is how a rainbow forms. Things look coloured because they absorb some colours of light and reflect the rest. Mixing coloured lights can make white, but mixing paints makes a dark, muddy colour. Nobody yet knows whether the red you see looks the same as the red someone else sees.
summary.art: A beam of white sunlight entering a glass prism on a windowsill and fanning out into red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet across a child's open palm.

intro.hook: Fill a clear glass to the top with water. Stand it at the edge of a windowsill where the morning or evening Sun shines in. Now look at the floor below it. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
intro.text: Sunlight looks plain and white. It lights up the kitchen and nobody thinks about it. But sometimes, after the monsoon rain, a giant curve of colours hangs in the sky. Where were those colours before the rain came? Were they in the clouds? In the water? Or were they hiding inside the sunlight all along? In 1666, about 360 years ago, a young man in England called Isaac Newton darkened his room to find out. He made a small hole in the window shutter and put a glass prism in the beam of sunlight.
intro.art: A dark room with a single bright beam coming through a small hole in a wooden shutter, a glass prism in its path, and a band of colours on the opposite wall.

outcomes: I can say that sunlight is many colours mixed together, and that things look coloured because they absorb some colours and reflect the rest.
I can use a prism or a glass of water to split light into colours, and name the colours in order.
I can explain that a rainbow forms when sunlight goes into raindrops, bends, bounces and comes out as colours.
I can say where to stand to see a rainbow: with the Sun behind me and rain in front of me.
I can mix the colours back into white with a spinning colour wheel, and say why mixing paints gives a dark colour instead.
I can run a fair test, write what I saw, and finish with claim, evidence and reasoning.
I can say what scientists agree about colour, and what nobody knows yet, like whether your red is the same as mine.
I can talk about light past the ends of the rainbow, what starlight tells us, and animals that see colours we cannot.

terms.meaning: Light is what lets us see. It comes from things like the Sun, a bulb or a flame.
terms.example: When you switch off the light at night, the room goes dark.
terms.art: A bulb and the Sun side by side, both shining.

terms.meaning: White light is light that has no single colour of its own. Sunlight is white light. It is really many colours mixed together.
terms.example: The light from the noon Sun on a white wall looks white.
terms.art: A white beam with tiny coloured threads twisted inside it, like a rope.

terms.meaning: Colour is how light looks to our eyes. Red, green and blue are colours.
terms.example: A ripe mango looks yellow. A leaf looks green.
terms.art: A mango, a leaf and a blue kite.

terms.meaning: A prism is a clear block, often glass, with flat sides at an angle. It splits white light into colours.
terms.example: A triangle-shaped glass prism on a sunny table throws a small rainbow.
terms.art: A triangle-shaped glass prism with a band of colours coming out.

terms.meaning: A spectrum is the band of colours you get when white light is split. The colours always come in the same order.
terms.example: A glass of water in sunlight can throw red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet in a line on the floor.
terms.art: A long strip of colours from red to violet, with no gaps.

terms.meaning: A rainbow is a curve of colours in the sky. It forms when sunlight shines into raindrops.
terms.example: After a monsoon shower in the late afternoon, a rainbow appears in the east.
terms.art: A rainbow over a wet green field with a cow and a cyclist.

terms.meaning: When light goes from air into water or glass, it changes direction a little. We say it bends. Scientists call this bending refraction.
terms.example: Light bends as it goes into a raindrop.
terms.art: A straight line of light that turns a little where it enters a block of water.

terms.meaning: To reflect is to bounce back. Light reflects off a mirror and off the inside of a raindrop. We see most things by the light they reflect.
terms.example: A mirror reflects your face back to you.
terms.art: A ball of light bouncing off the back wall of a water drop.

terms.meaning: Violet is the purple-blue colour at one end of the rainbow. It bends the most in a prism.
terms.example: Violet is the colour of some brinjal flowers.
terms.art: A small violet brinjal flower.

terms.meaning: Indigo is a deep blue. Isaac Newton named it as a rainbow colour, between blue and violet. The word means 'from India', because the blue dye came from an Indian plant.
terms.example: Blue jeans and some block-printed cloth are dyed indigo.
terms.art: A length of deep blue block-printed cotton drying in the sun.

terms.meaning: A colour filter is a clear coloured sheet. It lets some colours of light through and absorbs most of the others.
terms.example: Red cellophane from gift wrap, or a see-through red sweet wrapper, is a red filter.
terms.art: A torch beam passing through red cellophane and coming out red.

terms.meaning: Light travels in tiny waves. The wavelength is the length of one wave. Red light has longer waves than violet light.
terms.example: Red waves are almost twice as long as violet waves.
terms.art: Two wavy lines, a long lazy red one and a short tight violet one.

terms.meaning: Infrared is light just past the red end of the rainbow. Our eyes cannot see it, but we can feel it as warmth.
terms.example: A TV remote sends infrared light. A phone camera can sometimes see it.
terms.art: A TV remote with a faint glow at its tip, seen on a phone screen.

terms.meaning: Ultraviolet is light just past the violet end. Our eyes cannot see it, but bees can.
terms.example: Ultraviolet from the Sun can burn your skin on a beach.
terms.art: A bee looking at a flower that has a dark target pattern only bees can see.

terms.meaning: Mixing colours of light means sending them into your eye together. All the rainbow colours together look white. Red, green and blue light together look white too.
terms.example: A spinning rainbow wheel looks pale grey, nearly white.
terms.art: A paper disc of rainbow slices, spinning into a pale blur.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing at a time. Then we know what made the difference.
terms.example: We use the same glass and the same water. We only move where the glass stands.
terms.art: Two identical glasses of water, one in sun, one in shade, with a tick between them.

terms.meaning: Three parts of a scientist's answer. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
terms.example: I think sunlight has colours in it. I saw six colours on the floor. The water spread them apart.
terms.art: Three speech bubbles: a lightbulb, an eye and a gear.

terms.meaning: A photon is a tiny packet of light, far too small to see. Light comes in these packets.
terms.example: A small torch sends out more than a million billion photons every second.
terms.art: A torch beam made of countless tiny glowing dots.

terms.meaning: To absorb light is to take it in, so that it does not bounce back. The light's energy usually turns into warmth.
terms.example: A black dosa tawa absorbs almost all the light that falls on it, so it looks black.
terms.art: Sunlight arrows falling on a black tawa and vanishing into it, with small wavy heat lines rising.

terms.meaning: A pigment is a substance that gives paint, dye, skin or a leaf its colour. It absorbs some colours of light and reflects the rest.
terms.example: Turmeric has a yellow pigment. Leaves have a green pigment called chlorophyll.
terms.art: A bowl of turmeric powder and a fresh green leaf.

terms.meaning: Mixing paints puts their pigments together. Each pigment absorbs some colours, so together they absorb more. Many paints mixed make a dark, muddy brown.
terms.example: Yellow and blue paint make green, because green is the main colour that both of them reflect.
terms.art: A child's paint palette with blobs of yellow and blue, a green blob where they meet, and a muddy brown blob where every colour was mixed.

explanations.concept: Sunlight is many colours mixed together
explanations.definition: White light, like sunlight, is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. A prism or a raindrop can spread them apart.
explanations.description: Sunlight looks white, so we think it is one plain colour. It is not. It is a mixture of red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet light, all arriving together. When they arrive together, our eyes see white. When something spreads them apart, we see each colour on its own. Nothing paints the colours on. They were in the sunlight all along.
examples: A glass of water on a sunny windowsill throws a strip of colours on the floor.
A drop of water on a leaf in the morning can flash red, then green, as you move your head.
A cut-glass bottle stopper or a chandelier bead throws tiny rainbows round a room.
explanations.art: A white beam drawn as a rope, unravelling into six coloured threads.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: sunlight is many colours mixed together.

explanations.definition: A prism splits white light into colours because each colour bends by a different amount as it goes in and out.
explanations.description: A prism is a clear block with flat sides at an angle. When light goes from air into glass, it bends a little. It bends again when it comes out. This bending is called refraction. Each colour bends by a different amount. Violet bends the most and red bends the least. So colours that went in together come out in slightly different directions. A little way off, they have spread into a band. The unit on bending light explains why light bends at all.
examples: Red always lands at one edge of the band, and violet at the other.
A glass of water works like a round prism.
A thick glass paperweight or a diamond can split light too.
explanations.art: A triangle prism with one white beam going in and six coloured beams fanning out, violet bent most and red least.
explanations.context: A prism is a clear block of glass with flat sides. This card explains how it splits white light into colours.

explanations.definition: A rainbow forms when sunlight goes into raindrops, bends, bounces off the back of each drop, and comes out split into colours.
explanations.description: A rainbow is made by millions of raindrops, each one working like a tiny prism. Sunlight goes into a drop and bends. It bounces off the back of the drop. Then it bends again as it comes out. Each colour comes out at a slightly different angle. So from any one drop, only one colour reaches your eye. Drops higher up send you red. Drops lower down send you violet. Together, all those drops make the whole bow.
examples: After a monsoon shower, when the Sun comes out behind you, you see a rainbow on the dark clouds ahead.
The spray of a waterfall, like Jog Falls in Karnataka, often holds a rainbow.
A spray bottle set to a fine mist makes a small rainbow on a sunny balcony, with the Sun behind you.
explanations.art: A big cut-open raindrop showing a sunbeam going in, bouncing off the back, and coming out as red and violet rays going to a child's eye.
explanations.context: A rainbow is a curve of colours in the sky. This card explains how raindrops make it.

explanations.concept: Where to stand to see a rainbow
explanations.definition: A rainbow is a circle centred on the point exactly opposite the Sun, which is where the shadow of your head falls.
explanations.description: You can only see a rainbow with the Sun behind you and rain in front of you. Look at the shadow of your own head. The rainbow is a circle around that shadow. The bow is always the same size around it. That is why rainbows come in the early morning or late afternoon, when the Sun is low. At noon the Sun is too high, and the bow is below the ground. From an aeroplane, people sometimes see the whole rainbow as a full circle.
examples: Morning rainbows appear in the west. Evening rainbows appear in the east.
At noon in summer, you will almost never see a rainbow in India.
The higher the Sun, the lower the rainbow sits in the sky.
explanations.art: A child with the low Sun behind them, their shadow on the grass, and a rainbow arching around the shadow of their head.
explanations.context: This card explains why you see rainbows only in some places and at some times of day.

explanations.definition: Because each raindrop sends each colour in one direction, every person sees a rainbow made by a different set of drops.
explanations.description: Each drop sends one colour to one place. If you take one step to the side, different drops send colours to your eyes. So you and your friend, standing apart, see light from different drops. Each person sees their own rainbow. That is also why you can never reach the end of a rainbow. When you move, the rainbow moves with you.
examples: Walk towards a rainbow. It never comes nearer.
Two cameras a few steps apart photograph two slightly different rainbows.
Your left eye and your right eye see slightly different rainbows too.
explanations.art: Two children standing a few steps apart, each with their own faint rainbow drawn from a different set of drops.
explanations.context: This card is about a surprising fact: no two people ever see the same rainbow.

explanations.definition: A double rainbow has a second, fainter bow outside the first, made by light bouncing twice inside each drop, with its colours in the opposite order.
explanations.description: Sometimes there is a second, fainter rainbow outside the first. In the second one, the colours are the other way round. Red is on the inside. It forms when light bounces twice inside each drop, not once. Each bounce loses some light, so the second bow is dimmer. The sky between the two bows looks darker than the rest. It is called Alexander's dark band, after Alexander of Aphrodisias, a Greek thinker who wrote about it about 1,800 years ago.
examples: In the main bow, red is on the outside. In the second bow, red is on the inside.
The sky inside the main bow looks brighter than the sky outside it.
Very rarely, people see a third bow.
explanations.art: Two rainbows, one bright and one faint outside it, with the darker band of sky between them.
explanations.context: Sometimes there are two rainbows at once. This card explains the second one.

explanations.concept: How many colours are in a rainbow?
explanations.description: Most books say seven colours. But look closely and there are no lines between the colours. Red fades into orange, and orange into yellow. People have counted the colours very differently. So the number of colours is partly about the light, and partly about the names we choose.
examples: Some children count five colours. Some count eight.
Many languages name blue and green with one word.
A spectrum seen through a good instrument shows a smooth band with no gaps.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago
perspectives.explanation: He said the rainbow has three colours: red, green and a purple-blue. He also thought it was made by clouds working like mirrors.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in his book Opticks in 1704
perspectives.explanation: He named seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. At first he named five. He added orange and indigo partly to make seven, like the seven notes of a musical scale.

The colours change smoothly, with no steps. There are thousands of shades our eyes can tell apart. Seven is a useful way of naming them, not a fact about the light. Scientists who study languages still argue about how much our colour words change what we notice.

explanations.art: A rainbow strip with no borders, and three children each drawing their own lines on it in different places.
explanations.context: Books say a rainbow has seven colours. This card is about whether that is really true.

explanations.concept: What makes red different from violet
explanations.definition: The colour of light depends on its wavelength, the length of its waves. Red has the longest waves we can see and violet the shortest.
explanations.description: Light travels as tiny waves, much too small to see. The colour depends on how long the waves are. Red light has the longest waves we can see. Violet has the shortest. Red waves are almost twice as long as violet waves. Laid end to end, about 150 red waves or 250 violet waves would fit across the thickness of one sheet of paper. Light also comes in tiny packets called photons. A violet photon carries more energy than a red one.
examples: Red, orange and yellow have longer waves. Blue and violet have shorter waves.
Violet and ultraviolet light carry more energy, which is why ultraviolet can burn skin.
Red light from a bicycle reflector is made of long waves.
explanations.art: A ruler-like strip with long lazy red waves at one end and short tight violet waves at the other, a tiny packet glowing above each.
explanations.context: This card is about what is really different between one colour of light and another.

explanations.concept: Colours past the ends of the rainbow
explanations.definition: Infrared is invisible light beyond red, and ultraviolet is invisible light beyond violet. They are light just like the colours we see, with longer or shorter waves.
explanations.description: The rainbow does not really stop at red and violet. It goes on, but our eyes cannot see the rest. In 1800, William Herschel, an astronomer in England, put thermometers in the colours of a spectrum. One just past the red end, where there was no colour at all, got the warmest. He had found infrared light. In 1801, Johann Ritter in Germany found invisible light past the violet end. It darkened a special chemical. We call it ultraviolet. Bees can see ultraviolet light. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that bees can see but we cannot.
examples: A TV remote talks to the TV with infrared light.
Sunscreen protects skin from ultraviolet light.
Sunflowers and many other flowers have ultraviolet patterns that guide bees to the nectar.
explanations.art: A spectrum on a table with three thermometers, one in the dark just beyond the red end showing the highest reading.
explanations.context: The rainbow seems to stop at red and violet. This card is about light that lies past both ends.

explanations.definition: Things look coloured because they absorb some colours of the light falling on them and reflect the rest to our eyes.
explanations.description: A leaf does not make green light. Sunlight falls on it with all its colours. The leaf's green pigment, chlorophyll, absorbs most of the red and blue light, and the leaf uses that energy to make its food. Much of the green light is reflected, and some of it reaches your eyes. So the leaf looks green. A ripe tomato absorbs most colours and reflects red. A white shirt reflects nearly all the colours. A black bag absorbs nearly all of them, which is why it gets hot in the sun. The unit on how we see tells you more about light bouncing into our eyes.
examples: Under red light, a green leaf looks dark, because there is no green light for it to reflect.
A black umbrella gets hotter in the sun than a white one.
Turmeric looks yellow because it absorbs blue light and reflects the other colours.
explanations.art: Sunlight with all its colours hitting a leaf: green arrows are reflected to an eye, and red and blue arrows are absorbed into the leaf.
explanations.context: This card explains why a leaf is green and a tomato is red, using what we know about sunlight.

explanations.definition: Mixing all the colours of light together makes white light again.
explanations.description: If white light can be split into colours, can the colours be put back into white? Isaac Newton did it in the 1660s and 1670s. He split sunlight with one prism. Then he caught the colours with a lens and a second prism, and white light came out. You can do it with a spinning wheel. Colour a disc with rainbow slices and spin it fast. Your eye cannot keep up, so it mixes the colours. The wheel looks pale grey or nearly white. It is grey, not bright white, because each slice reflects only part of the light that falls on it.
examples: A spinning rainbow top looks pale while it spins fast.
Phone and TV screens make white from tiny red, green and blue dots very close together.
A second prism, turned the other way, can join the colours again.
explanations.art: Two prisms, the first fanning sunlight into colours, the second turned the other way and squeezing them back into one white beam.
explanations.context: Sunlight can be split into colours. This card is about joining the colours back into white.

explanations.concept: Is colour in the light or in us?
explanations.description: Light has wavelengths, but the light itself is not 'red'. Red is what happens when that light reaches an eye and a brain. Most people have three kinds of colour-sensing cells in their eyes. Each kind is best at a different part of the rainbow. The brain compares them and makes the colours we feel. Some people have only two kinds working. They mix up some colours, like red and green. The pink-purple called magenta is not in the rainbow at all. Your brain makes it when red and blue light arrive together, with no green.
examples: Magenta, the colour of many bougainvillea flowers, has no place of its own in the rainbow.
A mantis shrimp has 12 kinds of colour cells, but tests show it is worse than us at telling close colours apart.
John Dalton, an English scientist, described his own colour blindness in 1794.

perspectives.explanation: Colour is wavelength. Red light is light with long waves. The rest is just how eyes report it.
Colour is made by the brain. The same light can look different colours depending on what is around it. Magenta exists only in brains.
Even if we know everything about waves and brains, we may not know what red feels like to you. Nobody knows if your red and my red are the same. This is still an open question.

explanations.art: An eye with three little coloured cups inside it and a brain lit up, making a rainbow inside a thought bubble.
explanations.context: This card asks a big question: are colours out there in the world, or made inside us?

explanations.definition: Every kind of atom makes its own pattern of lines in a spectrum, so the split light of a star shows what the star is made of.
explanations.description: When scientists split the light from the Sun very finely, they see thin dark lines across the rainbow. Joseph von Fraunhofer, a German lens-maker, mapped hundreds of them in 1814. Later, scientists found that each kind of atom makes its own lines, like a fingerprint. In 1868, astronomers came to Guntur in Andhra Pradesh to watch a total eclipse of the Sun. Pierre Janssen and others saw a bright yellow line in the Sun's light that no one could explain. Norman Lockyer in England said it came from an element nobody had found on Earth yet. It was named helium, after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun. In 1925, Cecilia Payne, a young woman astronomer, used the split light of stars to show that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
examples: An old-style tubelight or a CFL bulb, not an LED, seen on the shiny side of a CD shows a few bright coloured lines, not a smooth rainbow.
Astronomers can tell what a star is made of without ever going there.
Annie Jump Cannon sorted hundreds of thousands of stars by their rainbows, at Harvard, more than 100 years ago.
explanations.art: A rainbow strip crossed by thin black lines like a barcode, with the Sun beside it and a magnifying glass over one line.
explanations.context: This card goes from your prism out to the stars. Their split light tells us what they are made of.

explanations.concept: Why the sky is blue and sunsets are red
explanations.definition: Air scatters blue light more than red, so the sky looks blue. At sunset the light crosses so much air that mostly red and orange reach us.
explanations.description: Sunlight passes through the air on its way to us. The tiny particles of gas that make up air scatter blue light more than red light. Scatter means to send off in all directions. So blue light comes at you from every part of the sky, and the sky looks blue. At sunset, sunlight travels a long way through the air. Most of the blue has been scattered away before it reaches you. Red and orange are left. In 1921, on a sea voyage between India and England, C.V. Raman wondered why the sea was so blue. He showed that water scatters blue light too. His later work on scattered light won the Nobel Prize in 1930.
examples: The noon sky is blue. The sky near the horizon at sunset is orange and red.
On the Moon there is no air, so the sky is black even in daytime.
28 February, the day Raman announced his discovery in 1928, is National Science Day in India.
explanations.art: A curved Earth with the Sun's light passing through a thin layer of air at noon and a thick layer at sunset, blue arrows scattering away.
explanations.context: This card uses what we know about the colours in sunlight to explain the blue sky and red sunsets.

explanations.concept: Mixing light is not like mixing paint
explanations.definition: Mixing coloured lights adds colours, so the mix gets brighter and can look white. Mixing paints puts pigments together, and between them they absorb more colours, so the mix gets darker.
explanations.description: Shine a red light and a green light on the same patch of white wall, and the patch looks yellow. Add a blue light, and it looks white. Each light adds more colours to what reaches your eye. Paint works the other way. Each paint has a pigment that absorbs some colours and reflects the rest. When you mix paints, each pigment absorbs its own colours, so less and less light is reflected. Mix many paints, and very little light comes back, so you get a dark, muddy brown. The spinning rainbow wheel is different. Its slices sit side by side, so the light they reflect mixes in your eye, as coloured lights do. That is why it looks pale grey, not brown.
examples: Phone and TV screens make white from tiny red, green and blue lights.
Yellow and blue paint make green, because green is the main colour that both paints reflect.
Colouring the same spot with every felt pen makes a dark brownish blot, not white.
explanations.art: Left: three torch beams, red, green and blue, overlapping on a wall into white. Right: blobs of paint on a palette stirred together into a muddy brown.
explanations.context: Sunlight's colours mix into white. This card explains why mixing paints does the opposite and makes a dark colour.

agreed.text: Sunlight is a mixture of many colours.
agreed.evidence: A prism splits it into colours. Newton showed that a second prism could join them back into white light.

agreed.text: Each colour bends by a different amount in glass or water. Violet bends most, red least.
agreed.evidence: In every prism, every glass of water and every rainbow, the colours come in the same order.

agreed.text: Rainbows form when sunlight bends and bounces inside raindrops.
agreed.evidence: Around 1300, Kamal al-Din al-Farisi in Persia and Theodoric of Freiberg in Germany each made a model raindrop, a glass ball full of water, and made rainbow colours with it. In 1637, Rene Descartes worked out the rainbow's angle.

agreed.text: There is light our eyes cannot see, past both ends of the rainbow.
agreed.evidence: Herschel's thermometer warmed up beyond the red in 1800. TV remotes, sunburn and bee vision all use this invisible light.

agreed.text: Each kind of atom makes its own pattern of lines in a spectrum.
agreed.evidence: Helium was found in the Sun's light in 1868, 27 years before it was found on Earth in 1895.

challenging.claim: A rainbow is made by clouds working like a mirror.
challenging.who: Aristotle, about 2,350 years ago. Many people accepted it for more than 1,500 years.
challenging.for: Rainbows do appear on clouds, and they look like a reflection of the Sun.
challenging.against: Al-Farisi and Theodoric showed, around 1300, that a single ball of water makes the colours. It is the drops, not the cloud as a whole.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where rainbows come from.

challenging.claim: A prism adds colour to white light, like a stain.
challenging.who: Many people before Newton, including some scientists of his time.
challenging.for: Thick glass often looks a little coloured, so it seemed the glass was colouring the light.
challenging.against: Newton passed one colour, like red, through a second prism. It stayed red and did not change. If glass added colour, the second prism would have changed it again. And the colours could be joined back into white.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea Newton argued against: that the prism makes the colours.

challenging.claim: Colours come from light meeting darkness, not from white light being split.
challenging.who: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, a German poet, in his book Theory of Colours, 1810.
challenging.for: Goethe noticed true things about how colours look, like coloured shadows and the colours at the edges of dark shapes. Artists still learn from him.
challenging.against: As physics, his idea does not work. Measurements of light show that white light really is a mixture.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous poet who disagreed with Newton about colour.

challenging.claim: There are exactly seven colours in the rainbow.
challenging.who: Many school books, following Isaac Newton.
challenging.for: Seven names are easy to remember, and they match the main bands most people notice.
challenging.against: The colours change smoothly with no edges. Newton chose seven partly to match the seven notes of music. Many people today leave out indigo.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a rainbow really has seven colours.

challenging.claim: Our colour words change which colours we can see.
challenging.who: Some scientists who study languages. Others disagree.
challenging.for: In some studies, people whose language has two words for light blue and dark blue, like Russian, tell those blues apart a little faster.
challenging.against: The difference is small. People everywhere can see the same colours, even if they name them differently.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the words we use for colours change what we notice.

challenging.claim: Some women can see more colours than other people, because they have four kinds of colour cells.
challenging.who: Gabriele Jordan and other scientists, in a study published in 2010.
challenging.for: Tests found at least one woman who could tell apart colours that look the same to most people.
challenging.against: Such people seem to be very rare. Scientists still argue about how many there are and how much more they see.
challenging.context: Most people have three kinds of colour cells in their eyes. This card is about people who may have four.

big_questions.q: Where were the rainbow's colours before the rain came?
big_questions.hint: Think of the glass of water on the windowsill. Did the water make the colours, or show them?

big_questions.q: If you and your friend each see your own rainbow, is there one rainbow or many?
big_questions.hint: Each drop sends each colour to one place only.

big_questions.q: Is your red the same as my red? How could we ever find out?
big_questions.hint: We both call a tomato red. But can you show me what red feels like to you?

big_questions.q: If nobody is looking, is there still a rainbow in the sky?
big_questions.hint: The light is still bending in the drops. But where would the bow be centred?

big_questions.q: Why do we say a rainbow has seven colours, when the colours have no edges?
big_questions.hint: Try drawing a line where green ends. Does everyone draw it in the same place?

big_questions.q: A bee sees ultraviolet. What colours might there be that no human has ever seen?
big_questions.hint: Think of the flowers with patterns that only bees can see.

big_questions.q: How can a star's light tell us what the star is made of, from so far away?
big_questions.hint: Each kind of atom draws its own lines in the rainbow, like a fingerprint.

big_questions.q: Mixing coloured lights makes white, but mixing paints makes a dark brown. Why would mixing do opposite things?
big_questions.hint: Coloured lights each add colours that reach your eye. What does each pigment in a paint do to the light?

big_questions.q: A leaf absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. So is green the colour the leaf keeps, or the colour it gives away?
big_questions.hint: Think of the leaf in red light. With almost no green light to reflect, how did it look?

big_questions.q: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi explained the rainbow 350 years before Newton. Why do so many books tell only Newton's story?
big_questions.hint: Think about which books were read in which countries, and which languages they were written in.

story.title: The Glass Raindrop
story.note: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi was a real Persian scientist. Around 1300 he explained the rainbow using a glass ball filled with water inside a dark room, in his book Tanqih al-Manazir, a revision of Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics. Yusuf, the glassblower's boy, and everything that happens to him are made up.
text: The glassblower's boy was called Yusuf, and he was not supposed to be in the dark room. Nobody was supposed to be in the dark room, except the scholar.

The scholar's name was Kamal al-Din. He had a grey beard and ink on all ten fingers. He had come to Yusuf's master with a strange order. He did not want a lamp, or a bottle, or a bowl for sherbet. He wanted a ball of glass, perfectly round, as big as a pomegranate, and hollow inside, with a tiny neck for filling.
"What is it for?" asked Yusuf's master.
"It is a raindrop," said the scholar. "A very large one. One that will hold still."

Yusuf's master laughed. But he made the ball. And because Yusuf had the steadiest hands in the workshop, it was Yusuf who carried it through the streets, wrapped in wool, and Yusuf who was told to stay and hold it.

The dark room was a storeroom with its shutters nailed closed. In one shutter there was a single hole, no bigger than a lentil. A thin rod of sunlight came through it and lay across the dust in the air, as straight as a spear.
"Fill it," said Kamal al-Din. Yusuf filled the glass ball with water from the well, slowly, so that no bubble stayed inside. Then he held it up in the rod of light.
Nothing happened. The water glowed. A bright spot of light shone on the far side of the ball. That was all.

"Higher," said the scholar. "Now turn. Slowly." He was not looking at the ball. He was crouched on the floor with his back to the hole, peering up at the ball from below, the way you might look at a bird.

They did this for three days. Kamal al-Din moved the ball, moved his head, wrote in his book, crossed out what he wrote, and moved again. He talked as he worked, mostly to himself. He spoke of a great scholar called Ibn al-Haytham, who had lived nearly three hundred years before. He spoke of the Greek, Aristotle, who said the rainbow was the cloud acting like a mirror. "But a cloud is not a mirror," he muttered. "A cloud is drops. Only drops. So the secret must be inside one drop."

Yusuf did not understand most of it. But he understood that his arms ached. On the third afternoon, when the scholar went out to eat, Yusuf set the glass ball on a stool in the light. He sat down on the floor near the shutter, with his back to the hole, just to rest.
And there, glowing on the glass, was a spot of red.
It was not a dull red. It was red like the inside of a pomegranate, red like the first coal in the morning fire. It sat on the edge of the ball like a jewel.
Yusuf held his breath. Where had it come from? The sunlight was white. The water was clear. The glass was clear. He had made the glass himself. There was no red in it anywhere.

He leaned to the side to look more closely. The red slid away, and a yellow took its place. He leaned a little more. Green. Then a blue, deep as indigo cloth. Then a violet that was almost not there. He leaned back. Yellow. Red.

He moved his head up and down, side to side, until he was dizzy. Each place he put his eye, the same drop gave him a different colour. It was as if the ball were throwing colours into the room in many directions, red this way, green that way, and his eye could only catch one at a time.
When Kamal al-Din came back, Yusuf was lying flat on the floor, laughing.
"It is not in the ball," Yusuf said. "It is not in the ball, sir. It is where you put your eye."
The scholar looked at him for a long time. Then he lay down on the dusty floor beside the glassblower's boy, his grey beard in the dust, and put his own eye where Yusuf's had been.
"Red," he said quietly. He moved. "Green." He did not say anything for a while.

That night he wrote for many hours. Yusuf heard the pen scratching through the wall where he slept. The scholar wrote that the light goes into the drop and bends. It strikes the back of the drop and comes back, and bends again on its way out. And each colour leaves at its own angle, so that one drop gives one colour to one eye. A rainbow, he wrote, is not one thing hanging in the sky. It is a great crowd of drops, and each drop sends you only the colour that leaves it towards the place where you stand. The drops higher up give you red. The drops lower down give you violet. Together they make the bow.
He did not write the name of the glassblower's boy. People did not write the names of glassblowers' boys.

Some weeks later the rains came. Yusuf ran out of the workshop with clay still on his hands, because the Sun had come out low behind him and the sky ahead was dark and full of drops. There it was, a great bow across the city, over the domes and the drying cloth and the donkeys in the lane.
His friend Hamid came running up beside him, pointing. "Look! Look at it!"

Yusuf looked at Hamid. Then he looked at the rainbow. He thought of the millions of drops, each one a little glass ball, each one throwing its colours out in every direction. Some of those colours were falling on his eyes. Different ones, from different drops, were falling on Hamid's.
"Yes," said Yusuf. "I see mine. Do you see yours?"
Hamid frowned at him, as if he had gone mad. But Yusuf only smiled, and stood very still, so that his rainbow would not move.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the colours were never in the glass, the water or the sky. They were in the sunlight all along, and the drop only spread them apart. Each drop sends each colour off at its own angle, so one drop gives one colour to one eye, and every person sees a rainbow made by different drops. The story also quietly asks who gets written into the history books.
ask: Yusuf made the glass ball himself, and the water was clear. So where did the red come from?
When Yusuf moved his head, the colour changed. Why?
Why did Kamal al-Din want a glass ball as big as a pomegranate, instead of looking at real raindrops?
What did Yusuf mean when he said, "I see mine. Do you see yours?"
The scholar did not write down Yusuf's name. Whose names do you think are missing from the stories of discoveries?
