games.title: Rainbow Line-Up
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about the colours in white light. Players collect colour cards and answer light questions, racing to build a whole rainbow in the right order.

printables.title: 36 colour cards: 5 each of red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, plus 6 white light cards
items: WHITE LIGHT: swap this for any colour you need

printables.title: 20 question cards
items: Which colour bends the most in a prism?
Where must the Sun be for you to see a rainbow?
What colour does a rainbow wheel look like when it spins fast?
In the main rainbow, which colour is on the outside?
Name one way to make a rainbow at home.
What colour does a green leaf look under red light?
What is the light past red that we cannot see?
What is the light past violet that bees can see?
Who explained the rainbow with a glass ball of water, around 1300?
Who split sunlight with a prism in the 1660s?
Why can you never reach the end of a rainbow?
Name a colour that is not in the rainbow.
Which gas was found in the Sun's rainbow before it was found on Earth?
TEST IT: hold red cellophane over a torch. What colour comes out?
TEST IT: spin a coloured disc on a pencil. What do you see?

printables.title: A rainbow strip for each player, with six empty boxes

rules: Shuffle the colour cards and deal 3 to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top question card. Answer it out loud. If your answer is right, take a colour card from the pile.
Put colour cards on your rainbow strip only in order, starting from red. You cannot put green down until you have red, orange and yellow.
A white light card can be split into any colour you need, because white light holds all the colours.
If you get a TEST IT card, everyone does the test. The first person to explain the result gets two colour cards.
The first player to complete a whole rainbow, red to violet, wins.

setup.art: Six empty boxes in a row on a strip of card, marked with small coloured dots from red to violet.
setup.caption: 1. Give each player a rainbow strip with six empty boxes.

setup.art: Two piles of cards, colour cards and question cards, face down in the middle of a floor mat.
setup.caption: 2. Put the colour cards and question cards in two piles.

setup.art: A child placing a green card in the fourth box of a strip that already has red, orange and yellow.
setup.caption: 3. Answer a question, win a colour, build your rainbow in order.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a rainbow strip. 2. Shuffle the colour cards and deal 3 to each player. 3. Put the question cards in a pile.
flow.say: Each of us is building a rainbow, in the right order, red first. You win colours by answering questions about light.
flow.kid: Get your rainbow strip. You get 3 colour cards. Win more by answering questions. Build red to violet, in order.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rainbow Line-Up. It is a card game where you build a rainbow by answering questions about light.

flow.do: Play a practice round with the question card 'Which colour bends the most in a prism?'.
flow.say: Practice question. Which colour bends the most in a prism?
flow.kid: Practice question. Which colour bends the most in a prism? Tap your answer.

check.q: Rainbow Line-Up practice round: which colour bends the most in a prism?
check.why: Violet bends the most and red the least. That is why the colours spread apart. If they all bent the same, a prism would make no rainbow at all. Picking red is common, because red is at the top of the rainbow. Correct answer wins a colour card.

flow.do: Play the game until someone completes a rainbow. Read each question aloud for younger players.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the card. If you're right, take a colour.
flow.kid: Take a question card. Answer it. If you are right, take a colour card.
flow.parent: Good answers sound like this. The Sun must be behind you. Sunlight is all colours mixed. A spinning rainbow wheel looks pale grey, nearly white. Red is on the outside of the main bow. Magenta is not in the rainbow. Helium was found in the Sun's light first.

check.q: Rainbow Line-Up: you need violet, and you have a white light card. Can you use it?
options: Yes, because white light holds all the colours, including violet
No, because white is not a colour
check.why: In the game, as in real life, white light can be split into any colour, because it is all the colours together. Picking 'white is not a colour' is half right. White is not one colour. It is all of them.

flow.do: When someone wins, ask everyone to say the colours of their strip aloud, in order.
flow.say: Let's say the whole rainbow together, red to violet.
flow.kid: Say your rainbow aloud: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet.
flow.think: Why must the colours go in this order, and never another?

games.title: The Bending Race
games.players: 3 to 7 players, played outdoors or in a big room
games.context: This is a running game that acts out a prism. Each player is one colour of light. When they cross the 'glass', each colour slows down and turns by a different amount, so the colours spread apart.

printables.title: 7 colour badges to pin on
items: WHITE: the Sun, who starts the race

printables.title: A chalk court
items: Glass zone: a big chalk triangle

printables.title: Where did each colour land?
items: Where it reached the finish wall

rules: Draw a start line, a big triangle for the glass, and a finish wall beyond it.
Each player pins on a colour badge. All the colours stand together on the start line, holding hands, as white light.
On 'Go', everyone walks together in a straight line to the glass.
Inside the glass, everyone lets go and walks slowly. Each colour turns a little to one side, by the number of small turns on its badge.
When you come out of the glass, walk straight to the finish wall.
Mark where each colour lands. Did the colours spread into a rainbow, in the right order?

setup.art: A chalk court on a terrace: a start line, a big chalk triangle in the middle and a long line at the end.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a start line, a big glass triangle and a finish wall.

setup.art: Six children holding hands on the start line, each with a different coloured paper badge.
setup.caption: 2. All the colours start together, holding hands, as white light.

setup.art: The children fanning out after the triangle, red turning least and violet most, landing in a spread along the finish line.
setup.caption: 3. In the glass, each colour turns by its own amount. They spread out.

flow.do: 1. Draw the court in chalk. 2. Give each player a colour badge. 3. Line up the colours on the start line, holding hands.
flow.say: Holding hands, all together, you are white light. Let's see what happens when white light goes through glass.
flow.kid: Pin on your colour badge. Hold hands with the others. Together, you are white light.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Bending Race. Each player is one colour of light, acting out what happens in a prism.

flow.do: 1. Say 'Go'. 2. Everyone walks to the glass. 3. In the glass, each colour makes its number of small turns to one side. 4. Then each walks straight to the finish wall.
flow.say: Into the glass! Slow down. Red, one small turn. Violet, six. Now out, and walk straight!
flow.kid: Walk to the glass. Let go of hands. Turn your number of small turns. Walk straight to the wall.
flow.parent: The game is a picture, not the full science. Real light slows down in glass, and each colour slows a slightly different amount, which makes each colour bend differently. Violet bends most.

flow.do: Mark where each colour landed on the finish wall. Read the order aloud.
flow.say: Who landed where? Read the order from one end. Is it a rainbow?
flow.kid: Where did you land? Say the order of colours from one end.

check.q: In the Bending Race, the colours started together but landed spread out. Why?
options: Each colour turned by a different amount in the glass
check.why: Each colour turned by its own amount in the glass, so they left in different directions and spread apart. That is just what a prism does to sunlight. Picking 'some ran faster' misses the point. Speed did not change where they landed. The turning did.

flow.do: Play once more, but this time make every colour take the same number of turns.
flow.say: What if every colour turned the same amount? Let's try.
flow.kid: Play again. This time everyone takes 3 turns. What happens?
flow.think: If all colours bent the same, would we ever see a rainbow?

items.p: What is sunlight made of?
items.why: Sunlight is a mixture of all the colours. A glass of water or a prism spreads them apart. Picking 'only yellow' comes from drawing the Sun yellow. Picking 'only white light' describes how sunlight looks, not what is in it.

items.p: You put a full glass of water on a sunny windowsill. Colours appear on the floor. Where did the colours come from?
opts: The colours were in the sunlight all along
items.why: The glass and water are clear. The water only spread out colours that were already in the sunlight. Picking 'the water is coloured' is a common first idea. Pour the water into a white cup to check.

items.p: A clear block of glass with flat sides that splits white light into colours is called a ____.
items.why: A prism splits white light because each colour bends by a different amount.

items.p: Put the rainbow colours in order, starting from red.
items.why: The colours always come in this order, because each one bends by its own amount. Red bends least and violet most.

items.p: Where must the Sun be for you to see a rainbow?
items.why: Raindrops send the colours back towards the side the Sun is on. So the Sun must be behind you. Picking 'in front' is the most common guess, because light comes from the Sun.

items.p: A rainbow is made by millions of raindrops.
items.why: True. Each drop works like a tiny prism and sends one colour to your eye.

items.p: In the main rainbow, which colour is on the outside of the bow?
items.why: Red is on the outside, at the top, and violet is on the inside. Picking violet mixes it up with the second, fainter rainbow, where the order is reversed.

items.p: You spin a disc coloured with all the rainbow colours. What does it look like while spinning fast?
items.why: Your eye mixes the light from all the slices, just as it mixes the colours in sunlight, so the disc looks pale grey, nearly white. Picking 'rainbow stripes' means thinking the eye can follow the fast spin. Picking 'black' mixes up light with paint. Mixed paints get darker, but the light from the slices adds up in your eye.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one split white light into colours, or not?
items: a glass of water in sunlight
items.why: Clear glass, water and tiny grooves can spread light into colours. Wood and cloth do not let light through to spread it.

items.p: Why can you never reach the end of a rainbow?
opts: It moves when you move, because it depends on where you stand
items.why: Each drop sends each colour to one place only. When you move, different drops make your rainbow. So it moves with you. Picking 'too far away' is a fair guess, but even close up, as with a spray bottle, it moves when you do.

items.p: A green leaf looks green because it reflects ____ light to our eyes and absorbs most of the other colours.
items.why: Sunlight has all colours. The leaf absorbs most of the red and blue light and reflects the green to our eyes.

items.p: In the Colour Filters activity, you hold red cellophane in the sunbeam. Which colour reaches the paper?
items.why: A red filter lets red light through and absorbs most of the others. Picking 'all the colours' means thinking the cellophane is just clear. Picking 'mostly green' mixes up which colour passes.

items.p: Match each thing to what it does.
pairs: makes one tiny part of a rainbow
items.why: Splitting, mixing and filtering are three things we can do with the colours in light.

items.p: When is the best time to look for a rainbow in India?
opts: At noon on a dry summer day
In the early morning or late afternoon, after a monsoon shower
In the middle of a dust storm
items.why: You need the Sun low and behind you, and rain in front of you. Picking noon forgets that the Sun is too high then. Picking midnight forgets that we need sunlight.

items.p: Draw yourself seeing a rainbow. Draw the Sun, the rain and the rainbow in the right places.
items.a: The Sun is behind the person. The rain and the rainbow are in front of them. Red is on the outside of the bow.
items.why: To see a rainbow, the Sun must be behind you and the rain in front.
items.art: A blank outdoor scene with a ground line.

items.p: Tell someone in two sentences why a glass of water makes colours on the floor.
items.a: Sunlight is all the colours mixed together. The water bends each colour a different amount, so they spread apart on the floor.
items.why: Any answer that says the colours are in the sunlight, and the water spreads them, is right.

items.p: In a prism, which colour bends the most?
items.why: Violet bends the most and red the least. That is why they spread apart. Picking red is common, because red is at the top of the rainbow.

items.p: In the water prism test, the glass, the mirror in water and the prism all gave the same order of colours. What is the best conclusion?
opts: The order comes from the light itself
All three were painted the same
items.why: Three different things gave the same order, so it must come from the light. Each colour has its own bending amount. Picking 'luck' would need three lucky results in a row.

items.p: A rainbow is part of a circle. Where is the centre of that circle?
opts: At the shadow of your head
At the top of the cloud
At the end of the rainbow
items.why: The rainbow is a circle around the point exactly opposite the Sun, which is where your head's shadow falls. Picking 'the Sun' is a common mix-up, but the bow is on the other side of the sky from the Sun.

items.p: Why do we hardly ever see rainbows at noon in summer?
opts: The Sun is too high, so the bow would be below the ground
items.why: The bow is a circle around your shadow's head. When the Sun is high, your shadow is short, and the whole bow is below the horizon. Picking 'raindrops are hot' guesses at the wrong cause.

items.p: From an aeroplane, you can sometimes see a rainbow as a full circle.
items.why: True. The ground usually hides the bottom half. From high up, with drops below you, the full circle can show.

items.p: In a double rainbow, how is the second bow different?
opts: It is brighter, with the same order
It is fainter, with the colours in the opposite order
items.why: The second bow comes from two bounces inside each drop. Each bounce loses light, so it is fainter, and the colours are flipped. Picking 'brighter' mixes up the two bows.

items.p: Under a red light in a dark room, a green leaf looks very dark, almost black. Why?
opts: There is no green light for it to reflect
items.why: A leaf looks green by reflecting green light. Red light has no green in it, so the leaf reflects very little and looks dark. Picking 'the leaf changes colour' forgets that it is green again in sunlight.

items.p: Some people counted 5 colours on a spectrum, and some counted 7. What does this tell us?
opts: The colours fade into each other, so the number depends on the names we choose
items.why: A spectrum has no lines in it. So the number of colours is about how we name them. Newton himself first counted five, then seven.

items.p: Light just past the red end of the rainbow, which we feel as warmth, is called ____.
items.why: William Herschel found it in 1800 with a thermometer, beyond the red end of a spectrum.

items.p: Light just past the violet end, which bees can see, is called ____.
items.why: Johann Ritter found it in 1801. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that guide bees.

items.p: Why is the sky blue in the daytime?
opts: Air scatters blue light more than other colours, sending it all over the sky
The sky is made of blue gas
items.why: The tiny particles of gas in air scatter blue light much more than red. So blue comes at us from every part of the sky. Picking 'the sea reflects onto it' is a very old idea. But the sky is blue over deserts too.

items.p: Match each person to what they found.
pairs: split sunlight with a prism and joined it back into white
explained the rainbow with a glass ball of water, around 1300
found infrared, past the red end, in 1800
showed that water scatters blue light, and studied scattered light
items.why: Many people in many countries, over many centuries, worked out the story of colour.

items.p: A white shirt and a black shirt hang in the sun. Which gets hotter, and why?
opts: The white one, because it reflects light
The black one, because it absorbs almost all the colours of light
Neither, because light has no energy
items.why: Black absorbs nearly all the colours, and the energy of that light turns into warmth. White reflects most of the light. Picking 'light has no energy' forgets that sunlight warms you.

items.p: In the story The Glass Raindrop, Yusuf said, "It is not in the ball. It is where you put your eye." What did he mean? Use what you know about rainbows.
items.a: Each drop sends a different colour in each direction. So which colour you see depends on where your eye is. When Yusuf moved his head, he caught a different colour from the same drop.
items.why: One drop gives one colour to one place. That is why every person sees their own rainbow.
items.context: The Glass Raindrop is this unit's story. Yusuf, a glassblower's boy, holds a glass ball of water in a sunbeam for a scholar.

items.p: Draw a prism with a white beam going in. Draw the colours coming out, in the right order. Show which colour bends most.
items.a: A white beam enters one side. Colours fan out of the other side, red bent least and violet bent most.
items.why: Each colour bends by its own amount. Violet bends most.
items.art: An empty triangle prism on a page.

items.p: Newton passed red light from one prism through a second prism. What happened?
items.why: A single colour does not split again. This showed that the prism does not add colours. It only separates the ones already in white light. Picking 'split into more colours' is what people who thought prisms make colours would expect.

items.p: How did Herschel find infrared light in 1800?
opts: He saw it with his eyes
A thermometer just past the red end got warmest
items.why: He put thermometers in the colours and just beyond them. The one past red, where there was no colour, warmed up the most. Picking 'saw it' forgets that infrared is invisible to us.

items.p: A tubelight seen through a spectroscope shows bright lines instead of a smooth rainbow. What do the lines come from?
opts: The particular atoms inside the tube, which each give out their own colours
items.why: Each kind of atom gives out its own colours, like a fingerprint. Tubelights contain a little mercury vapour. Picking 'dust' is a fair guess, but a clean tube shows the same lines.

items.p: Helium was found in the Sun before it was found on Earth. How?
opts: A yellow line in the Sun's split light did not match any known element
It was found in a balloon
items.why: In 1868, during an eclipse seen from Guntur in India, Pierre Janssen and other astronomers saw a yellow line in the Sun's spectrum. It matched no element known on Earth. Helium was found on Earth in 1895. Picking 'a balloon' is funny, because helium is now used in balloons, but it came later.

items.p: Magenta, the pink-purple of a bougainvillea flower, has its own place in the rainbow.
items.why: False. Magenta is not in the rainbow. Your brain makes it when red and blue light arrive together, with no green.

items.p: A mantis shrimp has 12 kinds of colour cells. Humans have 3. What did scientists find in 2014?
opts: Mantis shrimp see every colour much better than us
Mantis shrimp were worse than us at telling close colours apart
items.why: Hanne Thoen and her team found that mantis shrimp seem to recognise colours quickly but are poor at telling close shades apart. More colour cells does not always mean seeing more colours. Picking 'see every colour much better' is what most people guess.

items.p: Is your red the same as my red? Write what we could test, and what we might never be able to test.
items.a: We could test whether we both pick the same red from a set of colour cards, and whether our eyes have the same colour cells. We might never be able to test what red feels like inside you.
items.why: This is an open question. Scientists can measure light and eyes, but not yet what a colour feels like to someone.

items.p: Why are sunsets red, using what you know about sunlight?
opts: The Sun cools down in the evening
Sunlight crosses so much air that most blue is scattered away, leaving red and orange
items.why: At sunset, sunlight takes a long path through the air. Air scatters blue more than red, so by the time the light reaches you, mostly red and orange are left. Picking 'the Sun cools down' is a common idea, but the Sun is just as hot at sunset.

items.p: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi used a glass ball of water as a model raindrop. Why was a model useful?
opts: Real raindrops are too small and fall too fast to study
There was no rain in Persia
items.why: A real drop is tiny and gone in a moment. A big glass ball holds still, so you can study it. Picking 'models are always right' is not true. A model must be checked against the real thing.

items.p: Put these discoveries about colour in order, earliest first.
items: al-Farisi explains the rainbow with a glass ball
Cecilia Payne shows stars are mostly hydrogen and helium
Newton splits sunlight with a prism
a: al-Farisi explains the rainbow with a glass ball
Newton splits sunlight with a prism
Cecilia Payne shows stars are mostly hydrogen and helium
items.why: About 1300, then the 1660s, then 1800, then 1925. Discovery builds over centuries, in many countries.

items.p: A violet photon and a red photon. Which carries more energy?
items.why: Violet light has shorter waves and more energy in each packet. Ultraviolet has even more, which is why it can burn skin. Picking red is common, because red looks warm and hot.

items.p: Plants are green. What does that tell us about which light they use most for food?
opts: They absorb mostly red and blue light, and reflect green
items.why: A plant reflects the light it uses least. Green comes back to our eyes, so plants use mostly red and blue. Picking 'mostly green' is the most common mistake. Green is the light they absorb least.

items.p: A friend says: 'The rainbow is out there in the sky, in one place, and everyone sees the same one.' Give two pieces of evidence against this.
items.a: First, when you walk towards a rainbow, it moves with you, so it is not in one place. Second, each drop sends each colour in only one direction, so a person standing somewhere else gets colours from different drops. Also, in the spray rainbow test, when I took two steps sideways, the rainbow moved too.
items.why: A rainbow depends on where the viewer stands. Each person sees their own.

items.p: Which is the best fair test of whether water depth changes a water-prism's rainbow?
opts: Use different glasses and change the time of day
Use the same glass, same spot and same time, and change only how much water is in it
Try once with lots of water
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Changing the glass and the time too would mix up the causes. One try alone can be a fluke.

items.p: Newton said white light is many colours. Goethe, a German poet, said colours come from light meeting darkness. What experiment from this unit supports Newton? Explain.
items.a: Newton's Wheel. When the rainbow disc spins fast, all the colours mix back into pale white. So white really is all the colours together. Also, the water prism split sunlight into colours in the same order every time.
items.why: Splitting light into colours, and joining them back into white, both show that white light is a mixture.

items.p: Make up a question about colour or rainbows that nobody in your family can answer. How could you try to find out?
items.a: Any honest question with a sensible way to find out. For example: do dogs see rainbows? I could read about which colour cells dogs have.
items.why: Good scientists collect questions they cannot yet answer.

experiments.title: The Water Prism: do the colours ever change order?
experiments.context: This is the water prism test. You split sunlight into colours in three different ways: a glass of water, a mirror in a tray of water, and a glass prism if you have one. Then you check whether the colours always come in the same order.
experiments.question: When we split sunlight in different ways, do the colours always come in the same order?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the colours come in a different order with the mirror in water? Will red ever be in the middle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same sunlight, at the same time of day, and the same white paper. Only change the thing that splits the light. Look at each one twice, because a quick look can fool you.
results_table: Colours in the middle, in order

materials.item: a clear smooth glass, full of water
a small flat mirror and a shallow tray or baking dish of water
a glass prism, if you have one
white paper or a white wall
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, or at its reflection in the mirror. Point the mirror's light at the wall, never at anyone's face. A glass mirror's edges can be sharp, so a grown-up handles it.

schedule.what: Guess. Split sunlight three ways. Record the order of colours each time. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three strips of colours, one under the other, with red on the left each time.

setup.art: A full glass of water at the edge of a sunny sill, a strip of colours on white paper on the floor below.
setup.caption: 1. Split sunlight with a glass of water. Note the order.

setup.art: A small mirror leaning at a slant inside a tray of water, sunlight hitting it under the water, a rainbow strip on a white wall.
setup.caption: 2. Lean a mirror in a tray of water facing the Sun. Catch the colours on a wall.

setup.art: A triangle glass prism in a sunbeam on a table, a strip of colours on a sheet of white card.
setup.caption: 3. Try a glass prism too. Compare all three strips.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the glass, the mirror in the tray of water and the prism. 2. Ask them to guess whether the colours will come in the same order every time.
flow.say: We're going to split sunlight in three different ways. Do you think the colours will always come in the same order? Could red ever be in the middle?
flow.kid: You will split sunlight three ways. Guess first. Will the colours always be in the same order?
flow.context: This is the first step of the water prism test. You split sunlight in three ways and compare the order of the colours.

good: The colours are inside the sunlight, so they might always be the same.
The mirror is different, so maybe it will be different.

flow.do: 1. Stand the full glass at the edge of the sunny sill. 2. Catch the colours on white paper on the floor. 3. Write the colour at each end and the colours between them in the table.
flow.say: Which colour is at one end? Which is at the other? Let's write down the order, colour by colour.
flow.kid: Catch the colours on paper. Which colour is at each end? Write the order in the table.

flow.do: 1. Fill a tray with water and put it in direct sunlight. 2. Lean the mirror inside it at a slant, facing the Sun, so the sunlight hits the mirror under the water. 3. Move the mirror slowly until a rainbow strip lands on a white wall or card. 4. Record the order.
flow.say: This time the light goes into the water, bounces off the mirror, and comes back out. That's a little like what happens inside a raindrop. Let's see the order.
flow.kid: Lean the mirror in the water, facing the Sun. Find the colours on the wall. Write their order.
flow.parent: This works best with the Sun quite low and a white wall in the shade nearby. Tilt the mirror slowly. The water must be still, so wait a moment after moving it. The light goes in through the water, bounces and comes out, like light in a raindrop.

flow.do: If you have a prism, hold it in a sunbeam. Turn it slowly until a strip of colours falls on white card. Record the order.
flow.say: One more. A real glass prism. Turn it slowly. Same order or different?
flow.kid: Turn the prism slowly in the sunlight. Catch the colours on card. Same order?

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Compare the three rows of the table together.
flow.say: Look at all three rows. Did the order ever change?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Did the order ever change?

check.q: In the water prism test, the glass, the mirror in water and the prism all gave red at one end and violet at the other. What does this tell us?
options: Each thing paints its own colours
The colours and their order come from the sunlight itself
check.why: Three very different things gave the same colours in the same order. So the order must come from the light, not from the glass or the mirror. Each colour always bends by its own amount, red least and violet most. Picking 'each thing paints its own colours' would mean three different orders, which we did not see. Picking 'luck' is why we test more than once.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say three things. Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: sunlight always splits into the same colours in the same order. What I saw: with the glass, the mirror in water and the prism, red was at one end and violet at the other every time. Why: the colours are in the sunlight, and each one bends by its own amount.

experiments.title: Make Your Own Rainbow with a Spray
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a real rainbow with a plant spray bottle on a sunny balcony, terrace or doorstep, or with a garden hose if you have one. You test where you must stand to see it: with the Sun behind you, or in front of you.
experiments.question: Where must the Sun be for you to see a rainbow in the spray?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you see the rainbow better with the Sun in front of you, behind you, or beside you? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same spray, the same fine setting and the same time of day. Only change which way you face. Try each direction for one full minute.
results_table: Did I see a rainbow? (yes or no)
Where in the spray was it?
Which colour was on the outside?

materials.item: a plant spray bottle that makes a fine mist, or a garden hose with a fine-spray nozzle
a sunny morning before 9 o'clock, or an afternoon after 4 o'clock
a dark background, like a shaded wall, if you can find one

experiments.safety: Do this outside with a grown-up. Never look straight at the Sun. Spray away from people's faces and away from electric sockets and wires.

schedule.what: Guess. Spray with the Sun in front, beside and behind you. Record when you see a rainbow.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw yourself, the Sun, your shadow and the rainbow in one picture.

setup.art: A child on a sunny balcony facing the low Sun, spraying a fine mist from a spray bottle, with no rainbow visible.
setup.caption: 1. Face the Sun and spray. Is there a rainbow?

setup.art: The same child with the low Sun behind them, their long shadow on the ground, a bright rainbow arc in the spray ahead.
setup.caption: 2. Turn your back to the Sun and spray again.

setup.art: A grown-up and child crouching, the child's shadow head at the centre of a circle drawn around the rainbow.
setup.caption: 3. Find your shadow's head. The rainbow curves around it.

flow.do: 1. Go to a sunny balcony, terrace or doorstep in the early morning or late afternoon. 2. Set the spray bottle or hose to its finest mist. 3. Ask your child to guess where the Sun must be, and why.
flow.say: We're going to make a rainbow. Where should the Sun be, do you think? In front of us, beside us, or behind us?
flow.kid: You will make a rainbow with spray. Guess first. Where should the Sun be?
flow.context: This is the first step of the spray rainbow test. You find out where the Sun must be for you to see a rainbow.
flow.parent: You need direct sunlight on you and the spray. If your balcony gets no direct sun at these times, use the terrace or the building's entrance. Many homes already have a spray bottle for plants or ironing.

flow.do: 1. Face the Sun, but look down, never at it. Spray in front of you for one minute. 2. Turn so the Sun is to your side. Spray for one minute. 3. Write yes or no in the table each time.
flow.say: Let's try facing the Sun first. Don't look at it! Look at the spray. Any rainbow? Now let's turn sideways.
flow.kid: Face the Sun but look only at the spray. Any rainbow? Now turn sideways. Write yes or no.

flow.do: 1. Turn so the Sun is right behind you. 2. Spray the mist in front of you, a little higher than your head. 3. Look for the rainbow. Find the shadow of your head on the ground. Notice that the bow curves around it.
flow.say: Now the Sun is behind us. Spray up high. What do you see? Look down at your shadow. Where is your shadow's head?
flow.kid: Turn your back to the Sun. Spray high. Do you see the rainbow now? Find your shadow's head.
flow.parent: With the Sun behind you, a bow appears in the spray. It is part of a circle centred on the shadow of your head. Stretch out your arm: the bow is about two hand-spans from your shadow's head. Red is on the outside of the bow. If you see nothing, make the mist finer, spray in a different spot, or try a darker background.

check.q: In the spray rainbow test, when did you see the rainbow best?
check.why: Light goes into each drop, bounces off the back and comes back out towards the side the Sun is on. So you see it with the Sun behind you. Picking 'facing the Sun' is a common guess, because light comes from the Sun. But the drops send the colours back, like a mirror bounce.

flow.do: Ask your child to walk two steps to the side and look again.
flow.say: Take two steps to the side. Did the rainbow stay where it was, or come with you?
flow.kid: Take two steps sideways. Did the rainbow move with you?
flow.think: If your friend stands next to you, do you both see the same rainbow?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say three things. Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: you only see a rainbow with the Sun behind you. What I saw: facing the Sun there was no rainbow, but with the Sun behind me there was a bow around my shadow's head. Why: the drops bounce the light back towards the side the Sun is on, split into colours.

experiments.title: Newton's Wheel: spin the colours back into white
experiments.context: In this experiment you colour paper discs and spin them fast. You test which discs look white when spinning, to find out if the rainbow's colours can be mixed back into white.
experiments.question: If we spin all the rainbow colours together, will they look white?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess what colour each disc will look while spinning: the rainbow disc, the half-red half-green disc, and the all-red disc. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, make all the discs the same size, and spin them the same way and just as fast. Only change the colours on them. Spin each one three times.
results_table: Same as my guess? (yes or no)

materials.item: stiff card, like the side of an old box, with white paper glued on
a steel tumbler or small bowl to draw circles round
bright felt pens or colour pencils
a short pencil or a toothpick to spin the disc on
scissors, used with a grown-up

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the middle of each disc. Spin the discs on a table, away from faces.

schedule.what: Make three discs. Guess. Spin each one. Record the colour you see.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick your three discs on a page and write what each looked like while spinning.

setup.art: A round white card disc divided into six equal slices coloured red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round a tumbler. Colour six slices in rainbow order.

setup.art: The rainbow disc pushed onto a short pencil and spinning like a top on a table, looking pale grey-white.
setup.caption: 2. Push a short pencil through the middle. Spin it fast.

setup.art: Three spinning discs side by side: the rainbow one pale, a red-and-green one looking dull yellow-brown, an all-red one still red.
setup.caption: 3. Spin each disc. What colour do you see?

flow.do: 1. Draw three circles round a steel tumbler on white card. 2. Cut them out. 3. Divide the first into six equal slices, like cutting a round uttapam for six. Colour them red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. 4. Colour the second half red and half green. 5. Colour the third all red.
flow.say: Let's make three spinning wheels. This one is like Isaac Newton's colour wheel, with all the rainbow colours.
flow.kid: Draw three circles. Cut them out. Colour one with six rainbow slices. Colour one half red, half green. Colour one all red.
flow.context: This is the first step of Newton's Wheel. You make spinning paper discs to see if rainbow colours mix back into white.
flow.parent: To get six equal slices, fold the disc in half, then into three like a fan. Colour boldly and evenly. Felt pens work better than crayons. A grown-up pokes the hole in the centre with a sharp pencil.

flow.do: Ask your child to write a guess for each disc in the table.
flow.say: What colour do you think each one will look when it spins fast?
flow.kid: Guess. What colour will each disc look when it spins? Write it down.

flow.do: 1. Push a short pencil through the hole in each disc. 2. Spin each one like a top on the table, as fast as you can. 3. Spin each disc three times. 4. Write what you saw.
flow.say: Spin! What colour is it now, while it's spinning fast? Is it the same as your guess?
flow.kid: Spin each disc fast. What colour do you see? Spin each one three times.
flow.parent: The rainbow disc looks pale grey or creamy white, not bright white. Each slice reflects only part of the light that falls on it, so the mix is dimmer than white paper. It is still clearly paler than any of its colours. Red and green spun together look a dull yellowish brown. The all-red disc stays red.

check.q: In Newton's Wheel, the rainbow disc looked pale grey-white when it spun fast. What does this show?
options: When all the colours reach your eye together, they look white
The disc was really white all along
check.why: When the disc spins fast, every colour reaches your eye almost at the same moment. Your eye mixes them, just as it mixes the colours in sunlight. So you see a pale grey, nearly white. Picking 'spinning washes the colour off' is a fair guess. But the all-red disc stayed red when it spun, so spinning does not remove colour.

flow.do: Stop the rainbow disc and look at it again. Then compare all three discs.
flow.say: Look, the colours are still there! So where did the white come from?
flow.kid: Stop the disc. Are the colours still there? So where did the white come from?
flow.think: Sunlight is all the colours together. Is the white in sunlight one colour or many?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say three things. Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: all the rainbow colours together look white. What I saw: the rainbow disc looked pale white when it spun, but the all-red disc stayed red. Why: when all the colours reach my eye together, my eye mixes them into white, like sunlight.

activities.title: Catch a Rainbow on the Floor
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity, before anyone explains anything. You put a glass of water in the sunshine and look for colours on the floor. Then you look at a green leaf in red light.

materials.item: a clear, smooth glass, filled to the top with water
a sheet of white paper
a sunny windowsill or table edge, in the morning or late afternoon
a green leaf, from a potted plant, or a curry leaf or coriander leaf from the kitchen
red cellophane or a see-through red sweet wrapper, and a phone torch. Or, instead of both, a phone showing a plain red picture full screen

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Look only at the paper on the floor. Wipe up any spilt water.

schedule.what: Put the glass in the sun, catch the colours on paper, and talk about what you notice. Then look at a leaf in red light.

activities.record: Draw what you see on the paper. Colour it in the right order. Draw the leaf in red light and in room light. Write one thing you notice and one thing you wonder.

setup.art: A clear glass of water standing at the very edge of a sunny windowsill, with sunlight shining through it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a full glass of water at the edge of a sunny sill.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper on the floor below the windowsill with a small strip of colours on it.
setup.caption: 2. Put white paper on the floor where the light lands.

setup.art: A child on hands and knees moving the paper and pointing at a band of red, yellow, green and blue.
setup.caption: 3. Move the paper until you see colours. Look closely.

setup.art: In a dim room, a phone torch covered with folded red cellophane shining on a green leaf lying on white paper: the paper glows red and the leaf looks very dark.
setup.caption: 4. In a dim room, shine red light on a leaf on white paper.

flow.do: 1. Fill a clear glass to the very top with water. 2. Stand it at the edge of a sunny windowsill or table, so sunlight shines through it and down to the floor.
flow.say: Let's put this glass of water right here in the sunshine. Now don't tell me anything yet. Just look at the floor and the walls.
flow.kid: Fill a glass to the top with water. Put it at the edge of a sunny windowsill. Look at the floor below it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch a Rainbow. You find out what sunlight does when it goes through a glass of water.
flow.parent: If you see no colours, move the glass right to the edge, so light passes through it and down. Morning or late afternoon sun works best.

flow.do: 1. Put white paper on the floor where the light lands. 2. Move the paper slowly back and forth until a strip of colours appears.
flow.say: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Put white paper on the floor. Move it slowly. Can you see colours? Which colour is at each end?

good: There are colours on the paper.
Red is at one end and blue or violet is at the other.
The colours are in a row.
Where do the colours come from?
Why are they in that order?

check.q: The glass and water are clear. Sunlight looks white. So where do you think the colours on the paper came from?
options: The water has colour in it
The colours were hiding in the sunlight
check.why: The water is clear and the paper is plain white. The colours were already in the sunlight. The water only spread them apart. Picking 'the water has colour' is a very common first idea. Try pouring the water into a white cup. It has no colour. Picking 'nobody can know' is honest, but we can test it in this unit.

flow.parent: The strip is small, about the size of a finger, and often lies at the edge of the glass's shadow. Look along the edges of the shadow. If no window gets direct sun, put the glass on a step or wall in the sun outside, with the paper on the ground below.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the colours in order, and to write one thing they notice and one thing they wonder.
flow.say: Let's draw what we saw, in the right order. Then tell me one question you want to find out.
flow.kid: Draw the colours in the order you saw them. Write one question you have.
flow.think: If you put the glass in the shade, would you still see colours? Why or why not?

flow.do: 1. Go to a dim room. Put a green leaf on white paper. 2. Fold red cellophane or a red sweet wrapper two or three times, and hold it over a phone torch. If you have neither, open a plain red picture on a phone at full brightness. Use that screen as the light. 3. Ask your child to guess, then shine the red light on the leaf and the paper. 4. Switch the room light on again.
flow.say: This leaf is green and this paper is white. What colour do you think the leaf will look in red light? Why do you think so? Now look. Is the leaf brighter or darker than the paper?
flow.kid: Put a leaf on white paper in a dim room. Guess how it will look in red light. Shine the red light on it. Is the leaf brighter or darker than the paper?
flow.parent: The white paper looks bright red. The leaf looks much darker, a dull dark red or almost black. It may not look fully black, because cellophane lets a little other light through and a leaf reflects a little red. A darker room and folded cellophane make it clearer. Don't explain yet. The explanation cards come later.

ask.q: How did the leaf look next to the paper in red light?
good: The paper looked red, but the leaf looked dark.
The leaf did not look green any more.
When the light came on, the leaf was green again.

flow.think: The leaf was green again in room light. Did the leaf change, or did the light?

activities.title: Colour Filters: let only one colour through
activities.context: In this activity, you hold coloured see-through sheets in a sunbeam. Each sheet lets some colours through and absorbs most of the others.

materials.item: red, green and blue cellophane sheets, from gift wrap or a craft shop, or see-through coloured sweet wrappers
a glass of water in sunlight, or a glass prism
white paper
a torch

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, even through cellophane. Cellophane does not protect your eyes.

schedule.what: Make the strip of colours, then cover the beam with each coloured sheet in turn.

activities.record: Make a table with three rows: red sheet, green sheet, blue sheet. For each, write which colours still reached the paper.

setup.art: A glass of water on a sunny sill throwing a strip of colours onto white paper on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Make your strip of colours on white paper.

setup.art: A child holding a red cellophane sheet in the sunbeam before the glass, and the strip on the paper showing only red.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the red sheet in the sunbeam, before the glass.

setup.art: Three small pictures of the strip: one with only red, one with only green, one with only blue and violet.
setup.caption: 3. Try each sheet. Which colours are left?

flow.do: Make the strip of colours, as in Catch a Rainbow. Use a glass of water at the edge of a sunny sill and white paper on the floor.
flow.say: Let's make our strip of colours again. Today we'll test the colours with these coloured sheets.
flow.kid: Make the strip of colours again with the glass of water. Get your three coloured sheets ready.
flow.context: This is the first step of Colour Filters. You test which colours each coloured sheet lets through.

flow.do: 1. Hold the red sheet in the sunbeam, between the window and the glass. 2. Look at the strip on the paper. 3. Do the same with the green sheet, then the blue sheet.
flow.say: Before we try, guess. If the sunlight goes through red cellophane first, which colours will still reach the paper?
flow.kid: Guess first. Then hold the red sheet in the sunlight before the glass. What is left on the paper? Try green, then blue.
flow.parent: With red cellophane, mostly red and a little orange stay. With green, mostly green. With blue, mostly blue and violet. Cheap cellophane is not perfect, so a little of other colours may leak through. That is fine.

check.q: You hold red cellophane in the sunbeam. Only red reaches the paper. What happened to the green and blue light?
options: The cellophane turned them into red
They were never in the sunlight
check.why: The red sheet lets red light through and absorbs most of the other colours. It does not change green into red. Picking 'turned them into red' is a common idea. But then the red patch would grow wider and brighter. Instead, the green and blue patches just went dark. Picking 'never in the sunlight' forgets that we saw green and blue on the paper a minute ago.

flow.do: In a dim room, shine a torch through the green sheet onto a green leaf on white paper. Then shine it through the red sheet.
flow.say: Remember the leaf in red light, in Catch a Rainbow? Now let's try green light. Is the leaf bright or dark in green light? And in red light?
flow.kid: Shine the torch through the green sheet onto the leaf. Now use the red sheet. When does the leaf look bright?
flow.parent: In green light the leaf looks bright green. In red light it looks dark, a dull dark red or almost black. Cellophane leaks a little other light, so the difference may not be perfect, but it is easy to see.

ask.q: Why does the leaf look bright in green light but dark in red light?
good: Green light gives the leaf green to reflect.
In red light there is almost no green for the leaf to reflect.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say three things. Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the red sheet only lets red light through. What I saw: with the red sheet, the green and blue disappeared from the paper. Why: sunlight has all the colours, and the red sheet absorbed most colours except red.

activities.title: Bubble and CD Rainbows
activities.context: This activity is a rainbow hunt in soap bubbles and on a CD. These colours are made in a different way from a prism's, by very thin layers and tiny grooves.

materials.item: soap bubble mixture: a little dish soap in a cup of water
a straw or bubble wand
an old CD or DVD
a torch

activities.safety: Do not drink the soap water. Do not look straight at the Sun or the torch.

schedule.what: Blow bubbles in the light, look at the swirls, then tilt a CD under a torch.

activities.record: Draw a bubble with its colours. Draw the CD's rainbow. Write which one looks most like a prism's rainbow.

setup.art: A child gently blowing a big soap bubble through a straw, swirls of pink, green and gold on it.
setup.caption: 1. Blow a big bubble. Look at its swirling colours.

setup.art: A CD held under a torch in a dim room, a fan of rainbow colours on its shiny side.
setup.caption: 2. Tilt a CD under a torch. Watch the colours move.

flow.do: Blow a big soap bubble slowly. Hold it on the straw if you can. Look at its colours from close up.
flow.say: What colours do you see on the bubble? Are they the same as the rainbow on the floor?
flow.kid: Blow a big bubble slowly. Look at its colours. Do they move?
flow.context: This is the first step of Bubble and CD Rainbows. You look at colours made by very thin layers.
flow.parent: The colours on a bubble come from light bouncing off the inside and outside of a very thin soap skin. The two bounces join, and some colours grow brighter while others cancel out. Just before a bubble pops, its top often looks dark.

flow.do: In a dim room, shine a torch on the shiny side of a CD. Tilt it slowly.
flow.say: Now tilt the CD. What happens to the colours?
flow.kid: Shine a torch on a CD. Tilt it slowly. Watch the colours slide.
flow.parent: A CD has a tiny spiral groove, with thousands of lines in every centimetre. Light bouncing off the lines spreads into colours. This is called diffraction. It gives the same order of colours as a prism, but in a different way. Here red is spread out the most, the opposite of a prism.

check.q: A CD has no water and no prism. It still makes rainbow colours. What does this tell us?
options: CDs are painted in rainbow colours
There is more than one way to spread white light into its colours
check.why: Prisms, raindrops, thin bubbles and tiny grooves all spread white light into its colours, in different ways. Picking 'CDs are painted' is a good guess. But the colours slide and change as you tilt the CD, and paint does not do that. Picking 'only from water' is an idea this test proves wrong.

flow.do: Look for these colours around the house: on an oily puddle, a peacock feather, or the inside of a shell.
flow.say: Where else have you seen colours that move when you move?
flow.kid: Where else have you seen colours that change when you move? Make a list.
flow.think: A peacock feather is brown underneath. Why does it look blue and green?

activities.title: Where Does Green End? Counting the colours
activities.context: In this activity, each person in the family marks where they think each rainbow colour starts and ends. Then you compare. Books say the rainbow has seven colours. Is that true?

materials.item: a strip of colours, made with the glass of water or a prism on white paper
or a printed spectrum strip with no lines on it
a pencil for each person

activities.safety: Do not look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Each person marks the colours on their own copy, then everyone compares.

activities.record: Write how many colours each person counted. Draw a bar for each person.

setup.art: A long strip of smoothly changing colours from red to violet, with no lines on it.
setup.caption: 1. Get a strip of colours with no lines drawn on it.

setup.art: Three copies of the strip, each with pencil lines in slightly different places, and a number written at the end.
setup.caption: 2. Each person draws a line where each colour ends. Count them.

flow.do: Give each person a copy of the strip, or take turns marking the real one on paper. Ask them not to look at each other's.
flow.say: Draw a small line wherever you think one colour stops and the next begins. Don't peek at anyone else's!
flow.kid: Look at the colours. Draw a line where each colour stops. Do not peek at anyone else.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does Green End?. Everyone marks where they think each rainbow colour ends.

flow.do: 1. Count the colours each person marked. 2. Put the strips side by side. 3. Make a bar chart: one bar per person, as tall as the number they counted.
flow.say: How many colours did each of us count? Did we draw our lines in the same places?
flow.kid: Count your colours. How many did others count? Did you all draw your lines in the same places?

chart.title: Made-up example: how many colours each person counted
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your family's will be different.

check.q: Three people counted 5, 6 and 7 colours on the same strip. Who is right?
options: Only the person who counted 7, because books say so
Nobody, because the strip was wrong
Each count is a fair way of naming colours that have no edges
The person who counted 5, because fewer is simpler
check.why: The colours in a spectrum change smoothly, with no lines between them. So the number of colours depends on how we choose to name them. Picking '7, because books say so' trusts the book over your own eyes. Newton himself first counted five.

flow.do: Tell your child that Newton first named five colours, and later seven. He chose seven partly to match the seven notes of music, like sa re ga ma pa dha ni.
flow.say: Isaac Newton chose seven colours, partly because music has seven notes. If you were naming the rainbow, how many would you choose?
flow.kid: Newton picked seven colours, like the seven music notes. How many would you pick? Give them your own names.
flow.think: Is a colour a thing in the light, or a name we give it?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say three things. Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the rainbow does not have an exact number of colours. What I saw: we counted 5, 6 and 7 on the same strip. Why: the colours fade into each other with no edges, so we each drew our lines in different places.

activities.title: Sky Colour Diary
activities.context: In this 5-day activity, you look at the sky at noon and at sunset each day, and write down its colours. Then you explain the colours using what you know about sunlight.

materials.item: a notebook and colour pencils
a window, balcony or terrace where you can see the western sky at sunset

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, even at sunset. Look at the sky beside it. Go to the terrace only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Draw the noon sky and the sunset sky.
Compare all the drawings and explain the colours.

activities.record: Each day, colour a square for the noon sky and a square for the sunset sky. Write the time and the weather.

setup.art: A child on a terrace at noon, colouring a blue square in a notebook, the sky deep blue above.
setup.caption: 1. At noon, colour a square the colour of the sky.

setup.art: The same child at sunset, colouring an orange and pink square, the Sun low beside a water tank.
setup.caption: 2. At sunset, colour another square. Do it for 5 days.

flow.do: At noon, go outside and look up, away from the Sun. Colour a square for the sky. At sunset, look at the sky near the Sun, never at the Sun itself, and colour a second square.
flow.say: Let's be sky scientists for five days. What colour is the sky now? Let's match it with a pencil.
flow.kid: Look up at the noon sky. Do not look at the Sun. Colour a square to match. Do it again at sunset.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Sky Colour Diary. You record the sky's colours at noon and at sunset.

flow.do: On days 2, 3 and 4, add a sunset square each evening. Write the weather beside it.
flow.say: Is tonight's sunset the same as yesterday's? Is it a dusty day or a clear one?
flow.kid: Colour the sunset sky again tonight. Write if it is clear, cloudy or dusty.
flow.wait: Come back each evening for 3 more days

flow.do: On day 5, put the squares side by side and talk about the pattern.
flow.say: At noon the sky is blue. At sunset it is orange and red. Remember, sunlight has all the colours. Why might the blue go missing at sunset?
flow.kid: Look at your squares. Noon is blue. Sunset is orange. Where did the blue go?

check.q: At sunset, sunlight crosses much more air before it reaches you. Air scatters blue light away. What colours are left to reach you?
check.why: Air scatters blue light more than red. After a long trip through the air, most of the blue has been sent off sideways. Red and orange are left. Picking 'mostly blue' forgets that the blue gets scattered away on the long path. Picking 'only white' forgets that white is a mixture, and part of it has been removed.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say three things. Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the sunset is red because the blue light is scattered away. What I saw: every noon square was blue and every sunset square was orange or red. Why: sunlight has all colours, and at sunset it travels through so much air that mostly red and orange are left.

projects.title: Shoebox Spectroscope: the rainbows of lamps
projects.context: In this 3-day project, you build a spectroscope, a box that splits light into its rainbow so you can look at it closely. It uses a piece of old CD. Then you compare the rainbows of the Sun's light, a bulb, a tubelight and a candle.

materials.item: a shoebox or cereal box
an old CD or DVD, cut into a quarter by a grown-up with strong scissors
two pieces of card and black tape
scissors and glue, used with a grown-up
colour pencils and a notebook

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the CD, because the edges can be sharp. Never point the spectroscope at the Sun. Point it at a white wall lit by daylight. A grown-up lights and watches the candle.

schedule.what: Build the spectroscope. Test it on a white wall in daylight.
Look at a tubelight, an LED bulb and a candle. Draw each rainbow.
Compare the drawings and give a short 'rainbow show' to the family.

projects.record: Draw the rainbow of each light. Write whether it was smooth, or had bright lines or gaps.

setup.art: A cereal box with a thin slit cut in one end and a quarter of a CD taped at a slant over a hole at the other end.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a thin slit at one end and fix a piece of CD at the other.

setup.art: A child holding the box to their eye, pointing the slit at a glowing tubelight on the ceiling.
setup.caption: 2. Point the slit at a light. Look at the CD.

setup.art: Three drawn rainbows side by side: a smooth one for daylight, one with sharp bright lines for a tubelight, a warm red-orange smooth one for a candle.
setup.caption: 3. Draw each light's rainbow. Are they the same?

flow.do: 1. At one end of the box, a grown-up cuts a hole about 3 cm square. 2. Tape two pieces of card across it, leaving a slit as thin as a coin's edge. 3. At the other end, cut a viewing hole. 4. Tape the CD quarter inside at a slant, shiny side towards the slit. 5. Point the slit at a white sunlit wall and look at the CD.
flow.say: We're building a light-splitting box. The thin slit lets in a thin line of light, and the CD spreads it into its rainbow.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, cut a thin slit at one end. Fix the CD piece inside the other end. Point the slit at a bright wall. Look!
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Shoebox Spectroscope. You build a box that splits light into a rainbow you can study.
flow.parent: If you see no colours, tilt the box or the CD. The thinner the slit, the sharper the rainbow. A CD's tiny grooves spread light into colours in a different way from a prism, but you see the same order of colours.

flow.do: Look through the spectroscope at a tubelight, an LED bulb and a candle flame. Draw each rainbow in its own box in the notebook.
flow.say: Is the tubelight's rainbow smooth like daylight? Or does it have bright lines?
flow.kid: Look at a tubelight. Then a bulb. Then a candle, with a grown-up. Draw each rainbow.
flow.wait: Come back tomorrow, in the evening, when the lamps are on
flow.parent: Daylight gives a smooth rainbow. An old-style tubelight or CFL gives a rainbow with a few sharp bright lines, often green, orange-red and blue, because of the mercury vapour and the coating inside it. Many homes now have only LED lights. Look for a tubelight or CFL at a shop, a school or a relative's home. Rainbow glasses, if you buy them, do the same job as the box. An LED bulb or LED tube gives a smooth rainbow with an extra-bright blue part. A candle gives a smooth rainbow that is mostly red, orange and yellow, with little blue.

check.q: Through the spectroscope, a tubelight shows a few bright coloured lines instead of a smooth rainbow. What might that tell a scientist?
options: The light comes from a particular kind of atom, which makes its own lines
check.why: Each kind of atom gives out its own colours, which show as bright lines. The tubelight has mercury gas inside, and mercury has its own lines. This is how astronomers find out what stars are made of. Picking 'broken' is a fair first thought, but the tubelight is working fine.

flow.do: Lay out the drawings. Ask your child to explain each one to the family in a short 'rainbow show'.
flow.say: Tell us what you found. Which light had the smoothest rainbow? Which had lines?
flow.kid: Show your family your rainbow drawings. Tell them what you found.
flow.think: Astronomers look at stars this way. What could they learn from a star's rainbow?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say three things. Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: different lamps have different rainbows. What I saw: daylight was smooth, the tubelight had bright lines and the candle was mostly red and yellow. Why: each kind of light is made in its own way, by different atoms.

challenges.title: The Biggest Rainbow Indoors
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must make the biggest, brightest rainbow you can on a wall inside your home, using only things you find there.
challenges.problem: Your little cousin is coming to visit, and it is not raining. Make the biggest, brightest rainbow you can on a wall indoors, so they can stand in it.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
No paints, crayons or screens. The rainbow must be made of real light.
Measure your rainbow's width with a ruler each time you try a new idea.
materials: a glass of water, a tray of water and a small mirror
a torch, or a sunny window
white paper or a white wall
things to block extra light, like curtains or cardboard
general: Darken the room and let in just one strip of sunlight, so the rainbow stands out.
Put the white wall or paper further away from the water. The colours spread wider as they travel.
Use a mirror in a tray of water facing the Sun, and aim the colours at the wall.
creative: Make a slit in a piece of card, like the hole in Newton's shutter. A thin beam gives cleaner colours.
Try a round glass bowl full of water, like al-Farisi's model raindrop.
Try an old CD in a torch beam in a dark room. Its tiny grooves spread light into colours too.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, try it, and measure your rainbow. Is it bigger than the others?

setup.art: A dim room with curtains almost closed, one strip of sunlight falling on a tray of water with a mirror in it.
setup.caption: 1. Darken the room. Let in one strip of sunlight.

setup.art: A wide rainbow on a white wall with a child holding a ruler against it.
setup.caption: 2. Make the rainbow. Measure how wide it is.

setup.art: The same wall further away, with a much wider rainbow, and the child grinning.
setup.caption: 3. Change one thing. Is the rainbow bigger now?

flow.do: Read the challenge together. Look at the materials you have.
flow.say: Here's our job. Make the biggest rainbow you can, indoors, with real light. What do you think will make it bigger?
flow.kid: Your job: make the biggest rainbow indoors. Use real light. Think. What could make it bigger?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Biggest Rainbow Indoors. You plan how to make a big rainbow from sunlight.

flow.do: 1. Try your first idea. 2. Measure the rainbow's width with a ruler. 3. Change one thing, like the distance to the wall, and measure again.
flow.say: Let's try it and measure. Now let's change just one thing. Why only one?
flow.kid: Make your rainbow. Measure it. Change one thing. Measure again.
flow.parent: Changing one thing at a time keeps the test fair. The rainbow usually gets wider, but dimmer, as the wall gets further away. Keep children's eyes away from the mirror's reflected sunlight.

check.q: You moved the wall further from the water. The rainbow got wider but dimmer. Why?
options: The colours keep spreading apart as they travel, so the same light covers more wall
The water ran out of colours
check.why: Each colour leaves the water at a slightly different angle. The further they travel, the further apart they get. The same light spreads over a bigger patch, so it looks dimmer. Picking 'light gets tired' is a fun idea, but the light is not used up. It is only spread out.

flow.do: Show your cousin or family the best rainbow. Explain how it works in three sentences.
flow.say: Can you explain our rainbow to someone else? Where did the colours come from?
flow.kid: Show someone your rainbow. Tell them where the colours came from.
flow.think: Which idea surprised you most? Why did it work?

challenges.title: The Rainbow Forecaster
challenges.context: This is a thinking challenge. You use what you know about rainbows to say when and where to look for one in your town, so that nobody misses the next one.
challenges.problem: Your family keeps missing rainbows. Make a rainbow forecast card for your home. It should say which times of day, and which side of the sky, to look at after rain.
constraints: Your card must say the time of day and the direction to look.
It must work for morning and evening rain.
Use a drawing, not only words, so a small child can use it.
materials: a sheet of card and colour pencils
a compass, or a phone compass, or knowing where the Sun rises
your notes from the spray rainbow test
general: The Sun must be behind you, so in the morning look west, and in the evening look east.
The Sun must be low, so look before about 9 in the morning or after about 4 in the afternoon.
You need rain or spray in front of you, and sunshine behind you, at the same time.
creative: Draw a little clock face with the rainbow times shaded in.
Mark the rainbow side on a map of your home, like 'look out of the kitchen window in the evening'.
Add a monsoon reminder: in India, the best rainbows come with afternoon showers in the rainy season.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own forecast card. Stick it near a window. When you next see a rainbow, write the date and time on the card.

setup.art: A simple map of a home with arrows showing the morning Sun in the east and the evening Sun in the west.
setup.caption: 1. Find which way the Sun rises and sets at your home.

setup.art: A hand-drawn card with a clock showing shaded times, an arrow saying which window to look out of, and a small rainbow.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a card: when to look, and which way.

flow.do: Find out which side of your home faces east, where the Sun rises, and which faces west, where it sets.
flow.say: Where does the Sun rise at our house? Where does it set? Remember, for a rainbow the Sun must be behind you.
flow.kid: Where does the Sun rise at your house? Where does it set? The Sun must be behind you for a rainbow.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Rainbow Forecaster. You work out when and where your family should look for rainbows.

flow.do: Make the forecast card, with a clock and a direction arrow for morning and for evening.
flow.say: If it rains in the evening, which window should we look out of?
flow.kid: Draw your card. Show the time and which way to look, morning and evening.

check.q: It is 5 o'clock in the evening. The Sun is low in the west. Rain is falling. Which way should you look for a rainbow?
options: East, with the Sun behind you
check.why: You see a rainbow with the Sun behind you. In the evening the Sun is in the west, so you look east. Picking 'towards the Sun' is a common mistake. Remember the spray rainbow test: facing the Sun, there was no rainbow.

flow.do: Stick the card near the right window. Tell the family how to use it.
flow.say: Now everyone can be a rainbow forecaster. Let's tell them how it works.
flow.kid: Stick your card near the window. Tell your family how to use it.
flow.think: Why do we hardly ever see a rainbow at noon?

videos.title: What does the mantis shrimp see?
videos.why: The 2014 finding that an animal with 12 kinds of colour cells is worse than us at telling close colours apart. Good for the question 'is colour in the light or in us?'.
videos.check: Found by YouTube search: "What does the mantis shrimp see?" by Science Magazine. Title and channel checked automatically; a parent should preview it.

quiz.p: What is white sunlight made of?
quiz.why: Sunlight is all the colours mixed. A prism or a drop spreads them apart. Picking 'one colour, white' is what sunlight looks like, not what it is.

quiz.p: What does a prism do to white light?
opts: Spreads apart the colours already in it
quiz.why: Each colour bends by a different amount, so they spread apart. Picking 'paints colours' was an old idea. Newton showed a single colour does not change in a second prism.

quiz.p: Put these rainbow colours in order from red: blue, yellow, red, violet, green, orange.
quiz.why: The order is always the same: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. Red bends least and violet most.

quiz.p: Which colour bends the most in a prism or raindrop?
quiz.why: Violet bends most. If all bent the same, there would be no rainbow. Picking red is common, because red is on top.

quiz.p: What happens to sunlight inside a raindrop to make a rainbow?
opts: It goes in, bends, bounces off the back and comes out split into colours
quiz.why: Bend in, bounce off the back, bend out. Each colour leaves at its own angle. Picking 'it stops' forgets that the light comes back out to your eye.

quiz.p: You want to see a rainbow after an evening shower. Which way should you face?
opts: Away from the Sun, towards the east
quiz.why: The Sun must be behind you. In the evening it is in the west, so you face east. Picking 'towards the Sun' is the most common mistake.

quiz.p: You spin a rainbow-coloured disc fast. It looks pale white. What does this show?
opts: All the colours together look white
quiz.why: When all colours reach the eye together, we see white, as in sunlight. Picking 'spinning removes colour' is tested by the all-red disc, which stays red.

quiz.p: Why did we test each thing more than once in our experiments?
opts: Because one try can be a fluke
Because the first try is always wrong
quiz.why: Repeating a test makes sure the result is real. Picking 'the first try is always wrong' is not true. It may be right, but we cannot be sure from one try.

quiz.p: In the main rainbow, which colour is on the outside?
quiz.why: Red is on the outside and violet on the inside. In the fainter second bow, the order flips.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists NOT know yet?
opts: Whether your red looks the same to you as my red does to me
That rainbows are made by raindrops
That violet bends more than red
quiz.why: The other three are settled by experiments. What a colour feels like inside someone is still an open question.

quiz.p: A bee looks at a flower. What can it see that we cannot?
quiz.why: Bees see ultraviolet, just past violet. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that guide bees to nectar. Picking 'infrared' mixes up the two ends of the rainbow.

quiz.p: How do astronomers know what stars are made of?
opts: They split starlight into a rainbow and read the lines, which are like atom fingerprints
From the colour of the night sky
quiz.why: Each kind of atom makes its own lines in a spectrum. Cecilia Payne used this in 1925 to show stars are mostly hydrogen and helium. Nobody can visit a star. Stars are much too far away and too hot.

quiz.p: Why can't you reach the end of a rainbow?
opts: It moves with you, because it depends on where you stand
quiz.why: Each drop sends each colour to one place. When you move, different drops make your rainbow. Picking 'too high' misses that even a rainbow in a spray moves when you move.

quiz.p: You mix red, yellow, green and blue paint together in a cup. What colour do you get?
quiz.why: Each paint's pigment absorbs some colours. Mixed together, they absorb nearly all of them, so very little light is reflected. Picking 'white' mixes up paint with light. Coloured lights add up to white, but paints do not.

applications: Scientists split starlight into rainbows to find out what stars and planets are made of.
Doctors and laboratories use instruments called spectrometers to test blood, water and medicines by their colours.
Phone, TV and computer screens make every colour, and white, from tiny red, green and blue dots.
Stage lights at plays and weddings use colour filters to light a scene in one colour.
Traffic signals use red, amber and green lights that are easy to tell apart.
Prisms inside binoculars and cameras turn the light so the picture is the right way up.
The width and colours of a rainbow show how big the raindrops are. Very tiny drops, as in fog, make a pale, almost white bow called a fogbow.
Painters and dyers in India have used colours like indigo, turmeric and madder for thousands of years.
Remote controls use infrared light, just past the red end of the rainbow.
Sunscreen and sunglasses block ultraviolet light, just past the violet end.
Farmers and scientists use cameras that see infrared to check whether crops are healthy.
C.V. Raman's discovery about scattered light is used today to identify chemicals, even in old paintings.
