open_questions.q: Is the red you see the same as the red I see?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure light and eyes. But nobody knows how to measure what a colour feels like inside another person.

open_questions.q: Why do colours feel like anything at all?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know a lot about eyes and brains. But how brain signals become the feeling of red is one of the biggest puzzles in science, called the hard problem of consciousness.

open_questions.q: How many women can see extra colours, and how much more do they see?
open_questions.why_open: A few people may have four kinds of colour cells. They are rare and hard to find, and tests are difficult.

open_questions.q: How does the mantis shrimp's colour vision really work?
open_questions.why_open: It has 12 kinds of colour cells but is poor at telling close colours apart. Scientists have ideas but are not sure.

open_questions.q: Do our colour words change what we see?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find small effects. Others find none. Scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: What colours would we see if our eyes had more kinds of colour cells?
open_questions.why_open: Most people find they cannot imagine a truly new colour. We can only guess from animals that see more.

open_questions.q: What is light, really, if it acts like a wave and also like tiny packets?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists can predict what light does very well. But what it is underneath is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Exactly how did the first eyes that could see colour evolve?
open_questions.why_open: Eyes are soft and rarely leave fossils, so the early story is pieced together from living animals and genes.

maths.problem: In the Where Does Green End? activity, Amma counted 7 colours, Appa counted 5, the child counted 6 and Akka counted 6. Look at the chart. How many more colours did Amma count than Appa? Which number did most people count?
maths.answer: Amma counted 2 more than Appa. Most people counted 6.
maths.explain: Amma counted 7 and Appa counted 5. 7 take away 5 is 2. So Amma counted 2 more. Two people counted 6, and only one person counted each of the other numbers. So 6 is the number most people counted.
maths.context: In this activity, each person marked where they thought each rainbow colour started and ended, on the same strip of colours. Then they counted their colours.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many colours each person counted

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance that people disagreed, and by how much. That is the evidence that the rainbow has no exact number of colours.

maths.problem: In Newton's Wheel, you divided a disc into 6 equal slices, one for each colour. What fraction of the disc is red? If you made the wheel with Newton's 7 colours instead, would each slice be bigger or smaller?
maths.answer: Red is one sixth of the disc. With 7 colours, each slice would be smaller, one seventh.
maths.explain: The disc is cut into 6 equal parts, and red is 1 of them. So red is one sixth. If the same disc is shared between 7 colours, there are more slices, so each slice must be smaller. One seventh is smaller than one sixth.
maths.context: In Newton's Wheel, you colour a paper disc with rainbow slices and spin it fast to see whether the colours mix into white.
maths.why_maths: The slices must be equal so that no colour is stronger than the others. Fractions tell us how to share the disc fairly between the colours.

maths.problem: Rainbows only appear when the Sun is low. On one monsoon day, the Sun was low enough from 6 o'clock to 9 o'clock in the morning, and from 4 o'clock to 6:30 in the evening. How many hours in all could you have seen a rainbow, if it rained?
maths.explain: From 6 to 9 in the morning is 3 hours. From 4 to 6:30 in the evening is 2 and a half hours. 3 hours and 2 and a half hours make 5 and a half hours.
maths.context: In the spray rainbow test and the Rainbow Forecaster challenge, we found that you only see a rainbow when the Sun is low and behind you. These times are an example, not exact for every town.
maths.why_maths: A rainbow forecast needs times. Adding up time spans tells your family how long they have to look each day.

maths.problem: In the Biggest Rainbow Indoors challenge, a family measured their rainbow on the wall three times. With the wall 1 metre away, it was 4 cm wide. At 2 metres, it was 8 cm. At 3 metres, it was 12 cm. Look at the table. What is the pattern? How wide might it be at 4 metres?
maths.answer: It gets 4 cm wider for every extra metre. At 4 metres it might be about 16 cm wide.
maths.explain: 4, 8, 12. Each time the wall is 1 metre further away, the rainbow is 4 cm wider. 12 + 4 = 16. So at 4 metres it might be about 16 cm. It would also be dimmer, because the same light is spread wider.
maths.context: In this challenge, you try to make the biggest rainbow you can on a wall at home, and measure how wide it is.

chart.title: Made-up example: how wide the rainbow was

maths.why_maths: Finding the pattern lets you predict the next result before you measure it. Then you can test whether your prediction was right.

maths.problem: Red light waves are about 700 tiny steps long. Violet waves are about 400 of the same tiny steps. How many steps longer is a red wave than a violet wave?
maths.explain: 700 take away 400 is 300. So a red wave is 300 tiny steps longer than a violet wave. The tiny steps are called nanometres. A nanometre is so small that a million of them fit in one millimetre.
maths.context: In the water prism test, red always landed at one end and violet at the other. The difference between the colours is the length of their waves.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting tells us how different the two colours really are. That difference is why they bend by different amounts and spread apart.

roots.context: We have learned that sunlight holds many colours, and that things look coloured by absorbing some colours and reflecting the rest. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A glass of water split sunlight into a band of colours, from red to violet. White sunlight is all those colours together. A green leaf sends back green and takes in the rest, so under red cellophane it looked dark. So a thing can only show colours that are in what shines on it.
deep_truth.habit: We talk as if colour belongs to a thing, like its size: 'the leaf is green'. But a thing can only send back colours that are in the light that falls on it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the glass of water test, sunlight split into a band of colours. In Catch a Rainbow, a green leaf under a torch with red cellophane looked dark, and it was green again in daylight.

three.who_am_i: Your eye is part of every rainbow you see. When you step sideways, different drops send you their colours.
three.what_is_life: Life is fed by the colours in sunlight. A leaf absorbs red and blue light and uses its energy to make food.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of light we cannot see, beyond both ends of the rainbow. Bees see some of it.

roots.thread: Sunlight comes to us as one white light. A glass of water spreads it into many colours, and a spinning wheel mixes them back into white. The water adds no colour of its own. A leaf, a tomato and a shirt each send back a different part of the same sunlight. So every colour around us is one light, met by different things. The many things of the world come from one source in the same way: different on the outside, one underneath.

teachings.teaching: The teacher Uddalaka tells his son that the red colour of a fire belongs to heat, its white to water, and its dark to food. 'Fire' is only a name, he says. The three colours underneath are what is real.
teachings.link: Uddalaka looked under one name and found a mix of colours. A prism does the same with sunlight: under the one name 'white' are all the colours of the rainbow. His three colours are not the rainbow's, but the way of looking is the same.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Over the palace of the god Indra hangs a great net with a jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel, so each one holds all the rest.
teachings.link: Things around us do this with colour. Put a red cloth next to a white wall in sunlight, and the wall near it glows faintly red. So the light from the wall carries a little of the cloth too, as each jewel holds the others.

teachings.source: Jain teaching of anekantavada, many-sidedness, and the story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Each blind man touches one part of the elephant and says what it is. Each is partly right. No one view holds the whole truth.
teachings.link: Each person sees their own rainbow from their own place. No one sees the rainbow from everywhere at once.

science.text: White light is a mixture of all the colours we can see, and the colours can be split apart and joined back together.
Colour as we feel it is made by eyes and brains working together. Whether your red feels like my red is unknown.

other_view.view: White light is a mixture of waves of different lengths, and a rainbow is geometry in raindrops. They say this explains it fully, with no need for one source behind everything. That is an honest view.

practice.title: Colours with closed eyes
practice.say: Let's sit facing a bright window or the open sky, but not the Sun itself. Close your eyes gently. Notice that it is not black behind your eyelids. What colour is it? Maybe orange or red. That is sunlight coming through your eyelids. Your skin and blood absorb most of the other colours and let mostly red through. Now cup your hands over your eyes. Did the colour change? Take three slow breaths. Then open your eyes and look at a white wall. Remember, all the colours are in that white light.
practice.kid: Face a bright window, not the Sun. Close your eyes. What colour do you see? That red is sunlight coming through your eyelids. Now cover your eyes with your hands. Did the colour change? Breathe slowly three times. Then open your eyes.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought white light was pure and simple. They thought a prism added colours to it, perhaps by mixing in some darkness. Starting in 1666, a young Isaac Newton tested this. He darkened his room and let one thin beam of sunlight in through a small hole in the shutter. A prism spread the beam into a long strip of colours on the far wall. Then he let only one colour, such as red, pass through a small hole in a board. He sent that one colour through a second prism. If prisms added colour, the red should have changed again. It did not. It stayed red, and it bent by the same amount as before. Newton also used a lens to bring all the colours back together, and they made white again. He published his results in 1672. Some scientists, such as Robert Hooke, argued against him for years. But anyone could repeat the test, and it kept working. White light is not pure. It is a mixture of colours.
how_we_found_out.who: Isaac Newton, with Robert Hooke arguing against him
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A prism adds colours to pure white light. Newton sent a single colour through a second prism and it did not change, so the colours must already be in the light.
